extracted.intended_audience: employers, employees, labor unions, labor attorneys, human resources professionals, and NLRB practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: A regulatory standard (NLRB final rule) for determining when two or more entities are joint employers of particular employees under the National Labor Relations Act, including definitions, the types of control that do or do not establish joint-employer status, burden and bargaining obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Employer' / 'Employer of Particular Employees'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2(2) of the National Labor Relations Act defines an 'employer' to include 'any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly.' The rule grounds the joint-employer standard in the Act's definition of employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble stresses that the common-law meaning of 'employer' governs the Board's analysis and that interpretations should hew to established common-law agency principles as of 1935 and 1947. The threshold inquiry (§ 103.40(a) in the rule) asks whether a common-law employer-employee relationship exists between a putative joint employer and particular employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Joint Employers'
rubrics_metrics.description: An entity may be considered a joint employer of another employer's employees if the two 'share or codetermine the employees' essential terms and conditions of employment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule states that joint-employer status hinges on whether entities share or codetermine essential terms and conditions; this is the central definitional standard used throughout the rulemaking and explanatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'share or codetermine'
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'share or codetermine' means that two entities have authority over, or jointly decide, matters governing essential terms and conditions of employment for particular employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule explains that sharing or codetermining can include reserved authority, indirect control, or exercised control, and that the Board will look to the character and objects of such control (who may exercise it, when, and how) to determine whether the shared authority extends to essential terms and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Essential Terms and Conditions of Employment'
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms and conditions of employment that are central to the joint-employer inquiry — identified (in prior rule discussion) as wages, benefits, hours of work, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, and direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2020 rule had described an 'exhaustive' list of essential terms as including 'wages, benefits, hours of work, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, and direction.' The final rule grounds which matters are 'essential' in common-law agency principles and examines whether shared authority relates to such essential matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold common-law employer-employee relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Before addressing joint-employer status, the party seeking to demonstrate joint-employer status must first establish that a common-law employer-employee relationship exists between the putative joint employer and particular employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble and the rule direct parties to use established common-law indicators (primarily the right to control) to determine whether a threshold employment relationship exists (see § 103.40(a)). Only if that threshold is met does the Board proceed to analyze sharing/codetermination of essential terms (§ 103.40(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control sufficient to establish joint-employer status (authority/right to control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a putative joint employer's authority, right, ability, or power to control essential terms and conditions of employment (whether or not actually exercised) can be determinative of joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board emphasizes that the 'right to control' — including reserved contractual authority — is central under common-law agency principles. The rule gives 'determinative weight' to a putative joint employer's authority to control essential terms, without requiring proof that the control was actually exercised, and without regard to whether control is direct or indirect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved control (contractually reserved authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractually reserved authority to direct the manner in which work is performed (the right to control) can establish an employment relationship or joint-employer status even if that authority is not actually exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites Singer Mfg. Co. and other authorities to support that courts and restatements historically recognize that reserved rights to control suffice to create employer-employee relationships. The Board concludes it lacks authority to require an actual-exercise showing when reserved control exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect control, including control exercised through an intermediary
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect control or control exercised through an intermediary is relevant and may establish joint-employer status when it pertains to essential terms and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule and preamble note that indirect control can 'supplement and reinforce' evidence of an entity's authority to affect essential terms, and that case law has long recognized reserved and indirect control as probative in joint-employer analyses (e.g., Browning-Ferris decisions and subsequent cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual-exercise requirement is not necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board rejects a rule requiring showing of actual exercise of direct and immediate control; actual exercise is sufficient but not necessary to find a joint-employer relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains that the 2020 rule's 'actual-exercise' requirement is contrary to settled common-law agency principles. The Board will treat authority to control as determinative whether or not the authority was exercised, and irrespective of whether control is direct or indirect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and objects of control (who, when, how) (§ 103.40(c) inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: When analyzing whether a putative joint employer's authority extends to essential terms and conditions, the Board examines the character and objects of the control — i.e., who may exercise it, when they may exercise it, and how they exercise it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule directs fact-specific inquiry into the nature of the authority (not merely labels or formalities) to determine whether it bears on essential terms and conditions of employment for particular employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control immaterial to joint-employer status
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain forms or types of control that do not bear on the existence of an employment relationship or that do not affect essential terms and conditions are immaterial to joint-employer determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Table of Contents and rule text identify a section on 'Control Immaterial to Joint-Employer Status.' The Board will exclude forms of control that are immaterial (e.g., matters that do not affect wages, hiring, discipline, supervision, etc.) from the joint-employer analysis; the rule examines specific examples and doctrinal limits in that section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bargaining obligations of joint employers
rubrics_metrics.description: If entities are joint employers of particular employees, they share or bear obligations to bargain collectively under the NLRA with respect to those employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule includes a section on the bargaining obligations of joint employers and explains how joint-employer status affects duties to bargain and other NLRA responsibilities (including reference to Sec. 8(a)(5) consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of establishing joint-employer status
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule allocates the procedural burden for proving joint-employer status and explains how parties must proceed to meet that burden in representation and unfair labor practice contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble and the rule include a section on 'Burden of Proof' (or 'Burden of Establishing Joint-Employer Status') describing that the party asserting joint-employer status must first establish a threshold common-law employment relationship and then show that the character/objects of the putative employer's authority extend to essential terms. The rule explains evidentiary steps and analyses the Board will apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of established common-law agency principles as controlling baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board grounds the joint-employer standard in established common-law agency principles (as of 1935 and 1947), looking first to the 'right to control' and to judicial articulations and restatements of agency law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble repeatedly instructs reliance on primary judicial authority, Restatements, and secondary compendia to determine the scope of 'employer' and to inform which forms of control are legally significant. The Board rejects ad hoc administrative restrictions that conflict with historical common-law principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection/clarification of the 2020 rule's 'substantial direct and immediate control' test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board concludes that the 2020 rule's requirement of 'substantial direct and immediate control' (and excluding control that is 'only exercised on a sporadic, isolated, or de minimis basis') improperly narrowed joint-employer doctrine and is inconsistent with common-law principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble reviews the 2020 rule's formulation and explains why the Board rescinds those control-based restrictions, emphasizing that reserved and indirect control can be sufficient even when not direct or immediately exercised.
